questions.question: What two rules must a linear map $A\colon V\to W$ satisfy?
options: $A(u+v)=Au+Av$ and $A(\lambda u)=\lambda Au$.
$A(u+v)=Au+Av$ and $A(0)=0$.
$A(u+v)=Au+Av$ and $A(\lambda+u)=\lambda+Au$.
$A(u+v)=A(u)A(v)$ and $A(\lambda u)=\lambda Au$.

questions.question: Why is knowing a linear map on a basis enough?
options: Linear maps are defined only on finite sets.
Basis vectors must all be mapped to zero.
Every vector in the domain is a linear combination of basis vectors.
A linear map ignores all vectors outside the basis, so their images are never needed.

questions.question: What kind of object is $\mathcal{L}(V,W)$?
options: The set of all functions from $V$ to $W$, linear or not.
The vector space of all linear maps from $W$ to $V$.
The vector space of all linear maps from $V$ to $W$.
The set of invertible linear maps from $V$ to $W$.

questions.question: For a linear map $A$ with $A(e_1)=(1,0)$ and $A(e_2)=(0,3)$, what is $A(2e_1-e_2)$?
Why is the zero map $0(v)=0$ linear?
options: It sends $0$ to $0$, which is all linearity requires.
It satisfies both additivity and homogeneity.
Every constant map is linear, and it is constant.
Its kernel is $\{0\}$, so it preserves the structure.

questions.question: What is the quickest way to disprove that a map is linear?
options: Show it fails additivity for every pair of vectors.
Find one violation of additivity or homogeneity.
Find one input whose output is the zero vector.
Show that its matrix has determinant zero.

questions.question: Why must the domain and codomain be vector spaces over the same field for linearity?
options: Homogeneity uses the same scalars $\lambda$ in both $V$ and $W$.
Addition is used only in the domain, never in the codomain.
The definition requires both spaces to have the same dimension.
Otherwise the sum $Au+Av$ in $W$ would not be defined.

questions.question: Which map $T\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ is not linear because it does not send $\boldsymbol0$ to $\boldsymbol0$?
Which two differentiation rules from Math I show that the derivative map $\boldsymbol{D}(p)=p'$ on polynomials is linear?
options: $(pq)'=p'q+pq'$ and $(cp)'=cp'$
$(p+q)'=p'+q'$ and $(p\circ q)'=(p'\circ q)\,q'$
$(x^n)'=nx^{n-1}$ and $c'=0$ for constants $c$

questions.question: Which single condition on a function $\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to W$ is equivalent to $\boldsymbol{A}$ being linear?
options: $\boldsymbol{A}(\alpha\boldsymbol{u}+\beta\boldsymbol{v})=\alpha\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\beta\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}$ for all $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V$ and all scalars $\alpha,\beta$

$\boldsymbol{A}(\alpha\boldsymbol{u}+\beta\boldsymbol{v})=\alpha\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\beta\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}$ for all $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V$ and all scalars with $\alpha+\beta=1$

$\boldsymbol{A}(\alpha\boldsymbol{u}+\beta\boldsymbol{v})=\alpha\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}+\beta\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}$ for some $\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\in V$ and some scalars $\alpha,\beta$
$\boldsymbol{A}(\alpha\boldsymbol{u})=\alpha\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{u}$ for all $\boldsymbol{u}\in V$ and all scalars $\alpha$

questions.question: A linear map $\boldsymbol{f}\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2$ has $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{e}_1)=(2,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{e}_2)=(-1,3)$. Which matrix $\boldsymbol{A}$ satisfies $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}$ for all $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$
$\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$

questions.question: Why does every linear map $\boldsymbol{A}\colon V\to W$ satisfy $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{0}$?
options: Homogeneity with $\lambda=0$: $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{0}=\boldsymbol{A}(0\boldsymbol{v})=0\,\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{0}$.
It is an extra axiom of linear maps, checked separately from additivity and homogeneity.
It holds only for injective linear maps, where only $\boldsymbol{0}$ is sent to $\boldsymbol{0}$.
Every function between vector spaces sends $\boldsymbol{0}$ to $\boldsymbol{0}$, linear or not.
